sentences.text: Igai semkhu was a relatively slender titanosaur estimated to be 10 to 15 meters long, making it larger than the contemporary Mansourasaurus.
All preserved vertebrae feature opisthocoelus centra, a term for vertebrae with a concave rear surface, which possess large, deep, oval-shaped pleurocoels on their sides.
The fifth metacarpal possesses two distinct tubercles on its medial side, while the first and second metatarsals display distinct grooves; neither of these features are found in other titanosaurs.
The species name semkhu means 'the forgotten' in Ancient Egyptian, alluding to the specimen's complex history and the recent discovery of non-marine Cretaceous vertebrates in continental Africa.
Only one fossil occurrence of Igai has been recorded so far.
Igai fossils were first discovered in November 1977 by German researchers Karl Werner Barthel and Ronald Böttcher in the Kharga Oasis near the town of Baris in the Western Desert of Egypt.

The holotype specimen, VB 621–640, was sent to Germany in 27 plaster jackets after excavation, but the partial skeleton's preservation deteriorated due to preparation choices and insufficient storage.
Most of the Kharga specimen was transferred to the Museum für Naturkunde on September 11, 2008, excluding the left tibia and an isolated femur.
The genus Igai was named by Gorscak and colleagues in 2023, and the remains were formally named the new genus and species Igai semkhu that same year.
Igai belongs to the dinosaur family Saltasauridae and is classified within the dinosaur class Saurischia.

Phylogenetic analysis places Igai either as a relative of South American titanosaurs or within an Afro-Eurasian clade including Lirainosaurus and Opisthocoelicaudia, and researchers preferred the Afro-Eurasian classification for Igai, supporting the hypothesis that northern African Cretaceous taxa were related to European ones.
Igai lived during the Late Cretaceous in the Quseir Formation of Kharga Oasis, Egypt, and the dinosaur was found in the Quseir Formation of the Upper Cretaceous in the Jariyá Oasis, Egypt.
Igai lived approximately 74 to 72 million years ago during the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages, while other estimates place it during the Campanian stage between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
